summary: All three papers address polyp segmentation in colonoscopy images but adopt fundamentally different architectural philosophies. The transformer-based approach prioritizes accuracy, the lightweight CNN prioritizes efficiency, and the domain adaptation framework prioritizes generalization. Key tradeoffs emerge between accuracy, speed, and robustness across domains.

dimensions.name: problem

values.value: Improving segmentation accuracy for polyps with unclear boundaries
Enabling real-time deployment on resource-constrained hardware
Improving cross-domain generalization across different medical centers

dimensions.insight: Each paper addresses a distinct bottleneck in the clinical translation pipeline: accuracy, speed, and generalization.

dimensions.name: methodology

values.value: Transformer encoder with multi-scale attention decoder
Lightweight U-Net with depthwise separable convolutions
Domain adaptation with style transfer and domain discriminator

dimensions.insight: The papers span three different paradigms: transformers (paper-0), efficient CNNs (paper-1), and distribution alignment (paper-2).

dimensions.name: dataset
dimensions.insight: Kvasir-SEG is the only common dataset across all three papers, but paper-1 evaluates on it alone while others use multiple datasets.

dimensions.name: evaluation
dimensions.insight: paper-1 is the only paper that measures inference speed and model size, metrics critical for deployment.

dimensions.name: results

values.value: SOTA accuracy on multiple benchmarks; strong on boundary cases
Competitive accuracy with 93% fewer parameters; real-time speed
12% improvement in cross-domain setting; reduces annotation need

dimensions.insight: Each paper achieves the best result in its respective objective, but no single paper addresses all three goals.

dimensions.name: contributions

values.value: Novel attention decoder; SOTA results; open-source release
Style-based domain adaptation; cross-validation across centers

dimensions.insight: Contributions are complementary — the ideal system would combine accuracy (paper-0), efficiency (paper-1), and generalization (paper-2).

agreements: All three papers identify polyp segmentation as critical for early colorectal cancer diagnosis
All papers use Kvasir-SEG as at least one evaluation dataset
All papers acknowledge the gap between research performance and clinical deployment
contradictions: paper-0 prioritizes accuracy via complex transformers, while paper-1 sacrifices accuracy for efficiency via lightweight CNNs
paper-2 argues domain shift is the primary bottleneck, while paper-0 and paper-1 do not address this at all
keyInsights: No single paper jointly addresses accuracy, efficiency, and generalization — each focuses on one dimension at the expense of others
Only paper-1 reports deployment-relevant metrics (FPS, parameter count), suggesting a gap between research evaluation and clinical requirements
Kvasir-SEG is used universally, but paper-1's single-dataset evaluation limits the generalizability of its claims
